digest.component_or_area: completion verification framework, in-process vs external-harness agent scaffolding
propositions: Production in-process verifier and minimal free-tool harness agent are compared on identical corpus to measure whether completion verification unreliability stems from in-process scaffolding (step budget, structured tool surface, mid-loop contracts) or the task itself.

Arm B (minimal harness agent) achieved zero false-PASS verdicts on planted-unmet acceptance criteria but produced 5 false-FAIL rejections on real acceptance criteria (94.6% agreement vs Arm A's 100%), concentrating on epic AC7 (commit scope) and AC2 (enrichment data presence).
Arm B wall-time median (415.5 s) is approximately 3.2× slower than Arm A (131 s), driven by task-agent overhead including full test-suite executions chosen by the agent.

Predeclared GO decision rule requires Arm B false-PASS = 0 (met), Arm B total rejections strictly < Arm A (failed: 5 > 0), and Arm B median wall time ≤ 2× Arm A (failed: 415.5 > 262), triggering a NO-GO outcome.

Arm A spent $12.82 of the $20 Bedrock cap on new runs after reusing 6 control transcripts; dispatch stopped to avoid breaching the cap given run variance, leaving 3 of 6 variants with partial Arm A pairing (all 6 variants ≥1 Arm A rep).

External-harness verifier seam is not justified by this corpus evidence; production in-process scaffolding showed no unreliability on control data, while the 5 Arm B rejections reflect strict-literal AC interpretation on real coverage gaps (e.g. set_project commit scope, enrichment map assertions) rather than tooling constraints.
